description: Read-only, record-verified NE-10 passage bridges. Each route identifies exact CKL records and only sources attached to those records; this registry remains separate from authored CKL relationships.

bridges.explanation: John's prologue places the Logos with God 'in the beginning' and associates it with creation and life, read with Genesis alongside wider Jewish wisdom and word traditions.
bridges.uncertainty: Conceptual genealogy is debated; this is an interpretive association, not proof of direct borrowing or a single source.

bridges.explanation: Revelation 12:9 identifies its 'ancient serpent' with the devil and Satan; Genesis 3:1 names the serpent without those identifications.
bridges.uncertainty: Explicit later reception; do not read the later names back into Genesis original wording.

bridges.explanation: Genesis stations cherubim to guard the way to the tree of life; the later sanctuary text places cherubim in sacred space, offered as context rather than a physical description.
bridges.uncertainty: The texts assign distinct functions; the comparison does not establish one appearance for Eden cherubim.

bridges.explanation: Genesis stations cherubim to guard the way to the tree of life; the later sanctuary text places cherubim in sacred space, offered as context rather than a physical description.
bridges.uncertainty: The texts assign distinct functions; the comparison does not establish one appearance for Eden cherubim.

bridges.explanation: Genesis does not name Watchers; 1 Enoch and Jubilees develop that reading, and Jude angels are often read beside Genesis 6 and those traditions.
bridges.uncertainty: This reception route does not add Watchers to Genesis or show that Jude retells all Second Temple details.

bridges.explanation: In Job 1-2, ha-satan bears the Hebrew article and functions as accuser/adversary in the heavenly council; CKL compares Zechariah 3 and distinguishes later identifications with the devil.
bridges.uncertainty: Lexical role, literary function, and later theology are related but distinct questions.

bridges.explanation: Leviticus opens with YHWH calling Moses from the tent of meeting immediately after Exodus closes with cloud and glory filling the completed dwelling.
bridges.uncertainty: Narrative continuity is explicit; it does not settle compositional history.

bridges.explanation: Both passages associate Israel's departure from Egypt with judgment on Egypt's gods.
bridges.uncertainty: Neither text provides a plague-by-plague list of individual divine targets.

bridges.explanation: Hosea recalls Israel as God's son called out of Egypt; Matthew rereads Hosea 11:1 in Jesus' return from Egypt while Israel remains Hosea's referent.
bridges.uncertainty: Matthew is later figural reception and does not erase Hosea reference to Israel.

bridges.explanation: CKL identifies Paul's reuse of Hosea 13:14 within his later resurrection argument.
bridges.uncertainty: Hosea 13:14 is textually and rhetorically disputed; Paul reuse does not remove Hosea threat-filled context.

bridges.explanation: Mark 1:2-3 combines wording associated with Exodus 23:20 in a composite citation presented under an Isaiah heading.
bridges.uncertainty: The citation is composite and should not be flattened into a quotation from only one source.

bridges.explanation: Mark 1:2-3 combines wording associated with Malachi 3:1 in a composite citation presented under an Isaiah heading.
bridges.uncertainty: The citation is composite and should not be flattened into a quotation from only one source.

bridges.explanation: Mark 1:2-3 combines wording associated with Isaiah 40:3 in a composite citation presented under an Isaiah heading.
bridges.uncertainty: The citation is composite and should not be flattened into a quotation from only one source.

bridges.explanation: Most witnesses give the Synoptic form in Luke 3:22; Codex Bezae and patristic evidence preserve Psalm 2:7 wording.
bridges.uncertainty: This is a variant, not the reading of all manuscripts; textual evidence and christological interpretation are distinct.

bridges.explanation: Mark's temple action places wording from Isaiah 56:7 within its scriptural interpretation of prayer, nations, commerce, and judgment.
bridges.uncertainty: Keep the critique in its Jewish context; it does not authorize contempt for Judaism or sacred places.

bridges.explanation: Mark's temple action places wording from Jeremiah 7:11 within its scriptural interpretation of prayer, nations, commerce, and judgment.
bridges.uncertainty: Keep the critique in its Jewish context; it does not authorize contempt for Judaism or sacred places.

bridges.explanation: Mark's saying about the Son of Man giving his life as ransom is read alongside the servant's suffering and benefit to others.
bridges.uncertainty: CKL lists several possible readings and establishes no uncontested source or theory.

bridges.explanation: CKL reads Mark 13's Son of Man imagery with Daniel 7 in a discourse on temple destruction, suffering, uncertain timing, and watchfulness.
bridges.uncertainty: This is an interpretive connection, not a direct quotation or modern prediction chart.

bridges.explanation: Matthew applies Isaiah's Immanuel sign to Jesus' birth; Isaiah 7 addresses Ahaz during the Syro-Ephraimite crisis.
bridges.uncertainty: The immediate identity of the child and relation of Isaiah setting to Matthew reuse remain disputed.

bridges.explanation: CKL documents Acts 8:26-40 as later reception of Isaiah's suffering-servant passage.
bridges.uncertainty: Isaiah does not name the servant; collective, individual, prophetic, messianic, and christological readings persist.

bridges.explanation: CKL documents 1 Peter 2:21-25 as later reception of Isaiah's suffering-servant passage.
bridges.uncertainty: Isaiah does not name the servant; collective, individual, prophetic, messianic, and christological readings persist.

bridges.explanation: Both passages share close wording about Zion, divine instruction, international adjudication, and weapons transformed for agriculture.
bridges.uncertainty: Direction of dependence and a shared source remain debated.

bridges.explanation: Jeremiah 26 attributes Micah 3:12 to Micah of Moresheth and uses it in a later dispute over prophetic judgment.
bridges.uncertainty: Jeremiah is one narrated later use and does not replace Micah original setting.

bridges.explanation: Acts 7:42-43 explicitly quotes a Greek form of Amos 5:25-27, including forms rendered Moloch and Rephan.
bridges.uncertainty: The Greek form and textual history matter within Stephen argument about Israel worship history.

bridges.explanation: Acts 15:16-18 quotes a Greek form of Amos 9:11-12 and applies restored Davidic-tent language to the nations.
bridges.uncertainty: Acts fulfillment logic is debated; compare Greek wording with Amos restoration context.

bridges.explanation: Romans 1:16-17 links the gospel and revelation of God's righteousness to Habakkuk 2:4.
bridges.uncertainty: The wording and force of righteousness and faith/faithfulness remain disputed.

bridges.explanation: Romans 4 builds its Abraham argument around Genesis 15:6 and the scriptural promise narrative.
bridges.uncertainty: Paul argument belongs to its audience and must not become contempt for Jewish practice or Torah.

bridges.explanation: Galatians 3 invokes Genesis 12:3 as scriptural ground for Abraham, blessing, and the nations.
bridges.uncertainty: Paul later reading does not erase Genesis narrative or Jewish interpretation.

bridges.explanation: Galatians 3 invokes Genesis 15:6 as scriptural ground for Abraham, blessing, and the nations.
bridges.uncertainty: Paul later reading does not erase Genesis narrative or Jewish interpretation.

bridges.explanation: Galatians juxtaposes Deuteronomy 21:23 with Torah performance and the Messiah's crucifixion.
bridges.uncertainty: The CKL claim cautions that Galatians does not say Torah, Jews, or Jewish practice are themselves cursed.

bridges.explanation: Galatians juxtaposes Deuteronomy 27:26 with Torah performance and the Messiah's crucifixion.
bridges.uncertainty: The CKL claim cautions that Galatians does not say Torah, Jews, or Jewish practice are themselves cursed.

bridges.explanation: James pairs this scriptural figure with Abraham and argues that deeds enact or complete faith (Genesis 22:1-19).
bridges.uncertainty: The comparison belongs to James argument about faith and works.

bridges.explanation: James pairs this scriptural figure with Abraham and argues that deeds enact or complete faith (Joshua 2:1-21).
bridges.uncertainty: The comparison belongs to James argument about faith and works.

bridges.explanation: Nahum 1:2-3 adapts language associated with Exodus 34:6-7 while emphasizing jealousy, vengeance, patience, power, and refusal to acquit.
bridges.uncertainty: This is lexical adaptation, not a flattened contradiction or verbatim quotation.

bridges.explanation: Nahum 1:15 and Isaiah 52:7 share good-news messenger language; CKL calls them a parallel, not Paul direct source.
bridges.uncertainty: Shared imagery does not establish direct borrowing.

bridges.explanation: Romans 10:15 directly cites Isaiah 52:7; CKL calls Nahum 1:15 a related messenger parallel, not Paul direct source.
bridges.uncertainty: This preserves the distinction between Paul Isaiah citation and Nahum parallel wording.

bridges.explanation: Hebrews 7 interprets Genesis 14:18-20 through Melchizedek as a literary analogy for Jesus' enduring priesthood.
bridges.uncertainty: This later scriptural argument is not a neutral biography or uncontested historical identification.

bridges.explanation: Hebrews 7 interprets Psalm 110:4 through Melchizedek as a literary analogy for Jesus' enduring priesthood.
bridges.uncertainty: This later scriptural argument is not a neutral biography or uncontested historical identification.

bridges.explanation: Jude 4-18 and 2 Peter 2 have a close literary relationship in wording and sequence.
bridges.uncertainty: Direction and mechanism of dependence remain disputed; neither letter is simply a copy without its own voice.

bridges.explanation: The tabernacle instructions and the First Temple dedication both describe divine dwelling and holiness, while referring to distinct sanctuaries and settings.
bridges.uncertainty: The CKL note explicitly distinguishes sanctuary, First Temple, Christological metaphor, community metaphor, and new-creation referents; shared language does not make them identical.

bridges.explanation: John 2 uses temple language christologically; the CKL note relates it to sanctuary traditions while keeping the temple and Christological metaphor distinct.
bridges.uncertainty: The CKL note explicitly distinguishes sanctuary, First Temple, Christological metaphor, community metaphor, and new-creation referents; shared language does not make them identical.

bridges.explanation: Ephesians uses community-as-temple imagery; the CKL note places it in conversation with temple and Christological sanctuary language.
bridges.uncertainty: The CKL note explicitly distinguishes sanctuary, First Temple, Christological metaphor, community metaphor, and new-creation referents; shared language does not make them identical.

bridges.explanation: Revelation pictures God dwelling with humanity in new creation; the CKL note compares this with community-temple language while preserving distinct referents.
bridges.uncertainty: The CKL note explicitly distinguishes sanctuary, First Temple, Christological metaphor, community metaphor, and new-creation referents; shared language does not make them identical.
